success_patterns: Agents spotted the clue reproduced in a J! Archive, Jeopardy-dump or flashcard snippet (Love Story, Break a leg, Clifford Odets, Adirondacks). Even when the snippet was cut off before the answer, they took the answer from the other passages that repeated the clue's details.

For definition or description clues (a coin worth one-twentieth of a pound, a desert that is 30% sand, a late governor on a 1992 stamp), the agent chose the entity named in the title of the passages that matched the most clue details (Shilling (British coin), Earl Warren, Love Story (novel)). It dropped the parenthetical tag.
Constraints stated in the clue ('3-word', 'largest', 'late', 'northern New York') were used to check candidates, not just to find them.
Final answers were bare and short ('shilling', 'Sahara', 'Adirondacks', 'Earl Warren', 'The Simpsons'). No descriptors were added, and the anchor words in the clue were not repeated.

patch.reasoning: All 8 successes followed existing rules. Three habits recur but are not stated explicitly: (1) the passage titles and headwords that match several clue details usually name the answer, and the title's parenthetical disambiguator should be dropped; (2) a clue found verbatim without an answer still confirms the topic, so the answer comes from the other passages; (3) explicit size or number hints in the clue ('3-word') are cheap checks against wrong candidates. Each is short and low-risk, so it should not hurt the other rules.

edits.target: - Otherwise, build the answer from passages that match several of the clue's details.
edits.content: - Passage titles and headwords are strong evidence. When several passages whose titles or first lines echo the clue's details are all about one entity ('Shilling (British coin) - Wikipedia', 'Earl Warren - Wikipedia', 'Love Story (novel)'), that entity is the answer. Drop the parenthetical disambiguator and any ' - Wikipedia' suffix from the answer.

edits.target: Do not talk yourself out of a well-supported entity.
edits.content: - If the clue appears verbatim in a snippet with no answer visible (a J! Archive page or a Jeopardy question dump cut off after the clue), that only confirms which clue is being asked. Take the answer from the other passages that repeat the clue's distinctive details, and answer confidently from them.

edits.target: - If the context offers several candidates (a different player in the same article, a film and its song), pick the one that satisfies ALL distinctive details: exact numbers, team, years, place. Do not choose one that fits only some.
edits.content: - Use any form hints in the clue as a final check on the candidate: '3-word phrase' (count the words), 'this largest ...', 'late', a stated decade or year, or a letter count in parentheses. If the candidate violates a hint, pick another.
